job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Priority issues** (most urgent for Thursday's markup): items 1, 2, 9, 11, 12, and 19.

1. **§2(1)(A), tonnage threshold.** The definition covers only activity above 10,000 metric tons per year, so operations below that level are not "commercial" and fall outside §3. Operators could also run commercial-scale testing just under the line, or report tonnage in a way that keeps them below it. Consider a lower threshold, a cumulative measure across all operations, or a rule that any sale or export of recovered material counts as commercial.

2. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** This limits the threshold to one vessel, so an operator can split activity across several vessels, or across affiliated companies, and stay under the line for each. Replace it with "by any vessel or combination of vessels operated by the same person or its affiliates."

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "other mineral resources" are undefined.** It is unclear whether sediment disturbance, collection without lifting to the surface, or discharge of tailings counts as recovery, and whether minerals such as cobalt crusts, seafloor massive sulfides, or phosphorites are "other mineral resources." Define both terms broadly.

4. **§2(1)(A), 200-meter depth floor.** "At depths greater than 200 meters" does not say whether depth refers to the vessel's location, the water column, or the seabed being recovered. Activity at shallower depths is excluded entirely, which may leave gaps for shelf or seamount extraction. Specify what depth measures, and justify or remove the floor.

5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary" is undefined.** The bill does not say which Secretary decides, what "comparable" means, what procedure applies, or whether determinations can be reviewed in court. Vague delegations like this invite both agency delay and legal challenge. Name the agency, set criteria, require public notice and a deadline, and make determinations reviewable under the APA.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person" is narrow.** It covers only U.S. citizens and corporations organized under state law. It does not clearly reach foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or other U.S.-controlled entities. Expand the definition to include any entity organized under U.S. law or controlled by U.S. persons.

7. **§3(a), extraterritorial reach.** The prohibition applies to "any person in the United States" and to "U.S. persons anywhere," so foreign companies and foreign-flagged vessels operating in international waters or other countries' zones are not covered. Extend coverage to vessels flagged in the U.S., vessels operated by U.S. persons, and any activity that affects U.S. commerce or relies on U.S. ports or financing.

8. **§3(a), "engage in" is undefined.** It is unclear whether financing, insurance, equipment supply, chartering, port services, processing, or importing and selling resulting minerals are covered. Without those, a company could mine abroad and bring metals into the U.S. market. Define "engage in" to include these activities, or add a separate import and sale prohibition.

9. **§3(b), grandfathering of "mining conducted under an exploration license."** Exploration licenses are not commercial mining authorizations, but this clause could be read to let commercial recovery continue under one. "Issued" is also undefined, so it is unclear whether it covers licenses or contracts issued by other authorities. Limit the grandfather clause to non-commercial exploration, require the license to be in good standing, and set an end date.

10. **§3(b) and §8, no moratorium on new permits.** The grandfather cutoff is the date of enactment, so agencies could issue new exploration licenses between introduction and enactment and those licenses would be protected. Add a moratorium on new licenses, permits, and contracts starting on the date of introduction.

11. **§3(c), the environmental assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no limits on tonnage, duration, sales, or agency approval. Commercial-scale recovery could be labeled as assessment, which makes this the largest loophole in the bill. Define the term narrowly, cap the material that can be recovered, require advance approval and reporting, and bar sale of recovered minerals beyond testing.

12. **§4 and §5, no penalty for registration or reporting violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failure to register under §4(a) or to file reports under §4(b) carries no penalty. Add civil and criminal penalties for failure to register, failure to report, and false certifications.

13. **§4(a), registration has no deadline or defined role.** The bill sets no deadline for registration, does not require registration before operations begin, and does not say what NOAA does with the registration or whether it is public. "Operator" is also undefined. Add a deadline, a pre-operation requirement, a definition of operator, and a statement of what NOAA must do with registrations.

14. **§4(b), reports have no content requirements.** The bill does not specify what a quarterly report must contain, such as tonnage, location, depth, sediment discharge, plume monitoring, or biological monitoring. Reports are self-certified, not public, not audited, and not required for activity labeled as environmental assessment. Specify the content, make reports public, and require independent verification.

15. **§2(3) and §4, the 5,000-gross-ton "covered vessel" threshold.** The registry applies only to vessels above 5,000 gross tons, while the prohibition is defined by activity. Smaller vessels that exceed the mining threshold escape registration, and "equipped for" is undefined, so a vessel could be reconfigured without triggering coverage. Tie the registry to the activity definition, or apply it to any vessel engaged in seabed recovery regardless of size.

16. **§5(a), enforcement mechanics are missing.** The bill does not name an enforcing agency, grant injunctive relief, create a citizen-suit provision, or authorize seizure or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals. It also does not say whether "each day" applies to each vessel, each ton, or each day of continuing operation, and it has no inflation adjustment. Add each of these.

17. **§5(b), "willfully" is undefined.** The criminal standard is unclear, and the bill does not address responsible corporate officers or aiding and abetting. Define the mental state and add liability for officers and facilitators.

18. **§5(a) versus §8, conflicting effective dates.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 delays the Act's effective date by 180 days. It is unclear whether conduct during that window is penalized. Align the two provisions, and state the intended effective date for each.

19. **§7(a) versus §7(b), direct conflict.** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress passes a joint resolution, but §7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment regardless of that finding. This is the most serious problem in the bill, since industry could argue the prohibition lapses automatically. Remove the sunset, or make §7(b) expressly subject to §7(a).

20. **§7(a), the trigger is vague.** "Serious harm" is undefined, and nothing requires the National Academies report to be commissioned or delivered by a deadline. The bill also does not state how the joint resolution moves through Congress or whether it is presented to the President. Define the standard, set a deadline for the report, and specify the procedure.

21. **§6, the treaty obligation has no teeth.** The Secretary of State "shall seek to negotiate" an agreement, but there is no consequence for failure, no reporting to Congress, and "equivalent" is undefined. Add a reporting requirement, define the standard, and bar U.S. participation in any weaker framework.

22. **No severability, savings, or preemption clause, and no tie to existing law.** If one provision is struck, the rest may be read to fall with it. The bill also does not address the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, which provides for NOAA licensing of deep seabed mining. Industry could argue that licenses under that Act are protected or that this Act does not reach them. Add a severability clause and express language stating whether this Act supersedes, amends, or repeals the 1980 Act.

23. **Missing definitions.** Several key terms are undefined, including "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "recovery," "operator," "seabed," and "State." Each one is a potential basis for a challenge. Add a definitions section covering all of them.

**Caveats:** This is a drafting review, not legal advice. Before Thursday, ask Senate Commerce Committee legislative counsel to review items 5, 9, 19, and 22 in particular. Also confirm that the text above matches the October 6 manager's amendment, since I can only review what was pasted here.
